title: Book 5, Chapter 17 — Sixteenth Year of the War—The Melian Conference—Fate of Melos
paragraphs: The next summer Alcibiades sailed to Argos with twenty ships and seized the three hundred suspected persons who were still left of the Lacedaemonian faction. The Athenians at once lodged them in the neighboring islands of their empire. The Athenians also made an expedition against the isle of Melos. They had thirty ships of their own, six Chian and two Lesbian vessels, sixteen hundred heavy infantry, three hundred archers and twenty mounted archers from Athens, and about fifteen hundred heavy infantry from the allies and the islanders. The Melians are a colony of Lacedaemon who would not submit to the Athenians as the other islanders had. At first they remained neutral and took no part in the struggle. Afterwards, when the Athenians used violence and plundered their territory, they took up an attitude of open hostility. The generals Cleomedes, son of Lycomedes, and Tisias, son of Tisimachus, encamped in their territory with the armament described above. Before doing any harm to the land, they sent envoys to negotiate. The Melians did not bring these envoys before the people, but told them to state the object of their mission to the magistrates and the few. The Athenian envoys then spoke as follows:

Athenians. The negotiations are not to take place before the people. The reason is that, if we spoke straight on without interruption, we could deceive the ears of the multitude with seductive arguments that would pass unrefuted (we know that this is what our being brought before the few means). So what if you who sit there were to follow a method more cautious still? Make no set speech yourselves. Take us up on whatever you do not like, and settle that before going any farther. And first tell us whether this proposal of ours suits you.
The Melian commissioners answered:

Melians. We cannot object to the fairness of instructing each other quietly, as you propose. But your military preparations are too far advanced to square with what you say. We see that you have come to be judges in your own cause. All we can reasonably expect from this negotiation is war, if we prove to be in the right and refuse to submit, and slavery if we do not.

Athenians. If you have met to reason about guesses at the future, or for anything other than to consult for the safety of your state on the facts that you see before you, we will give over. Otherwise we will go on.

Melians. It is natural and excusable for men in our position to turn more ways than one, in thought and in speech. However, the question in this conference is, as you say, the safety of our country, and the discussion, if you please, can proceed in the way you propose.

Athenians. For our part, we shall not burden you with specious pretenses. We shall not claim a right to our empire because we overthrew the Mede, or say that we are attacking you now for some wrong you have done us. A long speech of that kind would not be believed. And we hope that you in return will not try to influence us by saying that you did not join the Lacedaemonians although you are their colonists, or that you have done us no wrong. Aim instead at what is feasible, keeping in view the real sentiments of us both. You know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

Melians. As we see it, at any rate, it is expedient (we speak as we are obliged to, since you tell us to leave right alone and talk only of interest) that you should not destroy what protects us all. That protection is the privilege, when in danger, of invoking what is fair and right, and even of profiting by arguments not strictly valid, if they can be made to pass current. You have as much interest in this as anyone, since your own fall would bring down the heaviest vengeance and give the world an example to meditate on.

Athenians. We are not frightened by the end of our empire, if it should end. A rival empire like Lacedaemon, even if Lacedaemon were our real antagonist, is not so terrible to the vanquished as subjects who attack and overpower their rulers on their own. That, however, is a risk we are content to take. Now we will show you that we have come here in the interest of our empire, and that what we are about to say is meant to preserve your country. We would gladly rule you without trouble, and see you preserved for the good of us both.
Melians. But how, tell us, could serving turn out as good for us as ruling would for you?
Athenians. Because you would have the advantage of submitting before suffering the worst, and we would gain by not destroying you.
Melians. So you would not consent to our being neutral, friends instead of enemies, but allies of neither side.
Athenians. No. Your hostility cannot hurt us so much as your friendship will, for your friendship would be an argument to our subjects of our weakness, and your enmity of our power.

Melians. Is that your subjects’ idea of equity, to put those who have nothing to do with you in the same category as peoples who are, most of them, your own colonists, and some of them conquered rebels?

Athenians. As far as right goes, they think that neither side has more of it than the other. They think that those who keep their independence do so because they are strong, and that we leave them alone only because we are afraid. So by your subjection we would not only extend our empire but gain in security. And because you are islanders, and weaker than others, it matters all the more that you should not get the better of the masters of the sea.

Melians. But do you think there is no security in the policy we indicate? Here again, you debar us from talking about justice and invite us to obey your interest, so we in turn must explain ours, and try to persuade you if the two happen to coincide. How can you avoid making enemies of all the neutrals who exist? They will look at our case and conclude that one day or another you will attack them. What is this but to make greater the enemies you already have, and to force others to become enemies who would never otherwise have thought of it?

Athenians. The fact is that continentals give us little alarm in general. The liberty they enjoy will long keep them from taking precautions against us. The ones more likely to take a rash step, and lead themselves and us into obvious danger, are islanders like yourselves who are outside our empire, and subjects who are smarting under the yoke.

Melians. Well then, if you risk so much to keep your empire, and your subjects risk so much to get rid of it, it would surely be great baseness and cowardice in us, who are still free, not to try everything that can be tried before submitting to your yoke.

Athenians. Not if you are well advised. The contest is not an equal one, with honor as the prize and shame as the penalty. It is a question of self-preservation and of not resisting those who are far stronger than you.

Melians. But we know that the fortune of war is sometimes more impartial than the disproportion of numbers might lead one to suppose. To submit is to give ourselves over to despair, while action still preserves for us a hope that we may stand erect.

Athenians. Hope, danger’s comforter, may be indulged by those who have abundant resources. They may suffer loss from it, but not ruin. Its nature, however, is to be extravagant, and those who go so far as to stake their all on it see it in its true colors only when they are ruined. As long as seeing it truly would let them guard against it, it is never found wanting. Do not let this happen to you, who are weak and hang on a single turn of the scale. Do not be like the vulgar, who throw away such security as human means may still afford, and when visible hopes fail them in extremity, turn to invisible ones: prophecies, oracles and other such inventions that delude men with hopes to their destruction.

Melians. You may be sure that we are as well aware as you how hard it is to contend against your power and fortune, unless the terms are equal. But we trust that the gods may grant us fortune as good as yours, because we are just men fighting against unjust. And we trust that what we lack in power will be made up by the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, who are bound, if only for very shame, to come to the aid of their kindred. So our confidence, after all, is not so utterly irrational.

Athenians. When you speak of the favor of the gods, we may as fairly hope for it as you. Our pretensions and our conduct are in no way contrary to what men believe about the gods or practice among themselves. We believe of the gods, and know of men, that by a necessary law of their nature they rule wherever they can. We did not make this law, and we were not the first to act on it. We found it already existing, and we shall leave it existing forever after us. We merely make use of it, knowing that you and everybody else, with the same power as ours, would do the same. So as far as the gods are concerned, we have no fear and no reason to fear that we shall be at a disadvantage. But when we come to your notion about the Lacedaemonians, your belief that shame will make them help you, here we bless your simplicity but do not envy your folly. When their own interests or their country’s laws are in question, the Lacedaemonians are the worthiest men alive. Much might be said about their conduct toward others, but no clearer idea of it could be given than by saying in a word that, of all the men we know, they are the most conspicuous in counting what is agreeable honorable, and what is expedient just. Such a way of thinking does not promise much for the safety on which you now unreasonably count.

Melians. But it is for this very reason that we now trust to their regard for expediency to prevent them from betraying the Melians, their colonists, and so losing the confidence of their friends in Hellas and helping their enemies.

Athenians. Then you do not take the view that expediency goes with security, while justice and honor cannot be followed without danger. And danger is something the Lacedaemonians generally court as little as possible.

Melians. But we believe that they would be more likely to face even danger for our sake, and with more confidence than for others. Our nearness to Peloponnese makes it easier for them to act, and our common blood ensures our fidelity.

Athenians. Yes, but an intending ally puts his trust not in the goodwill of those who ask his aid, but in a decided superiority of power for action. The Lacedaemonians look to this even more than others do. At least, they distrust their home resources so much that they attack a neighbor only with numerous allies. Is it likely, then, that while we are masters of the sea, they will cross over to an island?

Melians. But they would have others to send. The Cretan Sea is wide, and those who command it find it harder to intercept others than those who wish to elude them find it to slip through safely. And if the Lacedaemonians failed in this, they would fall upon your land, and upon those of your allies whom Brasidas did not reach. Then, instead of fighting for places that are not yours, you will have to fight for your own country and your own confederacy.

Athenians. You may one day experience a diversion of the kind you describe, only to learn, as others have, that the Athenians never once withdrew from a siege for fear of anyone. But we are struck by this. You said you would consult for the safety of your country, and yet in all this discussion you have mentioned nothing that men might trust in and expect to be saved by. Your strongest arguments rest on hope and the future, and your actual resources are too scanty, compared with those arrayed against you, for you to win. You will therefore show great blindness of judgment unless you can find some more prudent counsel than this once you have allowed us to retire. Surely you will not be caught by that idea of disgrace which proves so fatal to mankind in dangers that are both disgraceful and too plain to be mistaken. Too many men have their eyes perfectly open to what they are rushing into, and yet the thing called disgrace, by the mere influence of a seductive name, draws them on until they are so enslaved by the phrase that they fall willfully into hopeless disaster. They incur a disgrace more disgraceful because it accompanies error than when it comes as the result of misfortune. If you are well advised, you will guard against this. You will not think it dishonorable to submit to the greatest city in Hellas when it makes you the moderate offer of becoming its tributary ally, while you keep enjoying the country that belongs to you. And when you are given the choice between war and security, you will not be so blinded as to choose the worse. It is certain that those who do not yield to their equals, who keep terms with their superiors, and who are moderate toward their inferiors, on the whole succeed best. Think over the matter, therefore, after our withdrawal, and reflect again and again that you are consulting for your country, that you have only one, and that its prosperity or ruin depends on this one deliberation.

The Athenians now withdrew from the conference. The Melians, left to themselves, came to a decision in line with what they had maintained in the discussion, and answered: “Our resolution, Athenians, is the same as it was at first. We will not in a moment deprive of freedom a city that has been inhabited these seven hundred years. We put our trust in the fortune by which the gods have preserved it until now, and in the help of men, that is, of the Lacedaemonians, and so we will try to save ourselves. Meanwhile we invite you to allow us to be friends to you and foes to neither party, and to retire from our country after making such a treaty as shall seem fit to us both.”

Such was the answer of the Melians. As the Athenians left the conference, they said: “Well, you alone, as it seems to us, judging from these resolutions, regard what is future as more certain than what is before your eyes, and in your eagerness see what is out of sight as already coming to pass. You have staked most on the Lacedaemonians, and trusted most in them, in your fortune and in your hopes, and so you will be most completely deceived.”

The Athenian envoys now returned to the army. The Melians showed no signs of yielding, and the generals at once turned to hostilities. They drew a line of circumvallation round the Melians, dividing the work among the different states. Subsequently the Athenians returned with most of their army, leaving behind a certain number of their own citizens and of the allies to keep guard by land and sea. The force thus left stayed on and besieged the place.

About the same time the Argives invaded the territory of Phlius and lost eighty men, cut off in an ambush by the Phliasians and the Argive exiles. Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos took so much plunder from the Lacedaemonians that the Lacedaemonians, although they still refrained from breaking off the treaty and going to war with Athens, proclaimed that any of their people who chose might plunder the Athenians. The Corinthians also began hostilities against the Athenians over private quarrels of their own, but the rest of the Peloponnesians stayed quiet. Meanwhile the Melians attacked by night and took the part of the Athenian lines opposite the market. They killed some of the men, brought in grain and everything else useful that they could find, and then returned and kept quiet, while the Athenians took measures to keep better guard in future.

Summer was now over. The next winter the Lacedaemonians intended to invade the Argive territory, but on arriving at the frontier they found the sacrifices for crossing unfavorable, and went back again. This intention of theirs made the Argives suspicious of certain of their fellow citizens. They arrested some of them, but others escaped. About the same time the Melians took another part of the Athenian lines, which was only feebly garrisoned. Reinforcements then arrived from Athens under the command of Philocrates, son of Demeas, and the siege was pressed vigorously. Some treachery took place inside, and the Melians surrendered at discretion to the Athenians. The Athenians put to death all the grown men they took, sold the women and children as slaves, and afterwards sent out five hundred colonists and settled the place themselves.
